summary: Describes a set of MGCP packages that make use of the feature keys and displays on digital business phones and IP phones.

eli5.summary: It teaches a phone controller to use the buttons and screen on an office phone.

questions: how does mgcp control phone displays
what is the feature key package
subtitle: Extension packages to control feature keys, signals and XML displays on business phones.

tldr.problem: Basic MGCP supports only simple phones with dial pads and handsets, but modern business phones have feature keys, LCD displays and soft keys that need to be controlled by call agents.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three MGCP extension packages: Feature Key Package for buttons and indicators, Business Phone Package for speaker phone and beep signals, and Display XML Package for rendering UI on phone displays.
tldr.outcome: Call agents can now control business phone capabilities by commanding feature key states, labels and XML documents, enabling advanced features like Do Not Disturb and call display interfaces.

today: RFC 3149 is an Informational RFC describing extension packages that have been deployed in VoIP products, particularly for business phone integration with MGCP-based call control systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Business Phone Features
sections.content:
MGCP (Media Gateway Control Protocol) defined in RFC 2705 allows external call agents to control telephone gateways. However, the basic packages only support simple analog line endpoints, lacking support for the advanced features found on modern business phones.

A typical business phone includes feature keys (programmable buttons), line keys, an LCD display with soft keys, speaker phone capability, message and hold buttons, and microphone mute. Each business phone may have different hardware configurations. Rather than defining a fixed set of features, this RFC provides extension packages that allow applications to control these capabilities.

Three new MGCP packages are defined: Feature Key Package (KY), Business Phone Package (BP), and Display XML Package (XML). These work alongside the existing packages defined in RFC 2705 (Generic Media, DTMF, Line, and Handset packages).
sections.eli5: This adds instructions for how a phone's brain can control all the fancy buttons and screens on a business phone, not just simple dial pads.

sections.title: Feature Key Package
sections.content:
The Feature Key Package (KY) groups events and signals for feature keys on business phones. It defines three main elements:

Feature Key Events (fk1-fk99): These events map to all keys on the phone that are not DTMF keys or locally implemented (like volume). When a user presses a feature key, the phone reports which key was pressed (identified by number fk1 through fk99) to the call agent.

Key State Signal (ks): The call agent can set the state of a feature key by sending a signal with parameters for key number and state. States include enabled (en), disabled (db), idle (id), dial tone (dt), connected (cn), disconnected (dc), ringing (rg), ringback (rb), holding (ho), and held (he). Different phone hardware can interpret these states using their available indicators (LEDs, LCD text, icon colors, blink patterns).

Set Label Signal (ls): For phones with an LCD next to feature keys, this signal allows the call agent to set a label (up to the phone's character limit) next to a specific feature key. For example, setting the label to '2200' next to fk1 identifies it as the extension 2200.
sections.eli5: Think of buttons on your phone: the protocol tells the controller which buttons were pressed, lets it light them up or change their color, and lets it put names next to them so you know what they do.

sections.title: Business Phone and XML Display Packages
sections.content:
The Business Phone Package (BP) provides signals for phone functions not related to feature keys. It includes:

Force Offhook (hd): Activates the speaker phone and puts the phone in offhook state. This is used when a feature key triggers a call or when an application on a user's PC selects a number to dial.

Force Onhook (hu): Forces the phone onhook, used when the far-end disconnects or a feature key terminates a call.

Beep: Plays a beep on the phone for alerts or confirmations.

The Display XML Package (XML) allows the call agent to send XML documents to phones with displays. The XML framework uses WML (Wireless Markup Language) plus custom tags to define user interfaces. The call agent sends an XML signal with a URL to a deck (XML document), a card identifier, and variable substitutions. When users interact with the display (selecting items, entering text), the phone posts an XML event back to the call agent with the user's input.
sections.eli5: These packages let the controller make the phone turn on its speaker, play sounds, and show interactive menus on the screen that users can click through.

sections.title: XML Documents and Display Components
sections.content:
XML documents consist of decks and cards. A card defines a single user interaction, similar to a page in an application. Cards support multiple components: text boxes for display-only content, enumerated list boxes for scrollable selections, itemized list boxes for soft key selections, input boxes for user text entry, and echo boxes for displaying keypad input without consuming it.

Cards can include timers, call timers (incrementing duration displays), and dynamic content like the current time. Variables from the call agent (like the caller's name prefixed with $) are substituted before rendering. Event handlers using <do> tags trigger actions when the user makes selections or timers expire, such as navigating to another card or posting data back to the call agent.

For example, a card might display a list of options with soft key mappings, allowing a user to select an item. The selection triggers an onpick action that sends the selected value back to the call agent. Support for previous card navigation allows users to back out of display flows.
sections.eli5: The XML system is like a way to draw interactive menus on the phone screen. You can have lists to pick from, text boxes to type in, buttons for each choice, and timers that auto-advance to the next screen.

sections.title: Endpoint Naming and Local Implementation
sections.content:
Display endpoints are addressed separately from phone endpoints using a 'disp/' prefix. For example, if the phone endpoint is 'ep1@foo.whatever.net', the display endpoint is 'disp/ep1@foo.whatever.net'. This allows asynchronous control of the display while signaling the phone for calls.

Some functions should be implemented locally on the gateway rather than controlled by the call agent: volume control for ringing, handset and speaker phone; audio path switching between speaker phone and handset; and microphone mute button functionality.

The call agent must determine phone capabilities (which feature keys are available, whether an LCD exists) at startup. An experimental parameter 'X-UA' (User Agent) is defined for the Requested-Info field of the AUEP method. When queried, the phone responds with a string identifying its make and model, allowing the call agent to look up what features are supported.
sections.eli5: The display gets its own address so the controller can manage it separately from the phone. Some buttons like volume are handled by the phone itself. The controller asks the phone 'who are you?' at startup to know what buttons and screens it has.
